description: Top-level comments from a public Facebook group post (Nov 2026) asking how to close Maine's projected 2028-29 budget gap. Names removed; authors replaced with stable pseudonymous keys. Replies are not included. Gold labels are a single human-reviewed first pass and should be re-reviewed by a second labeler before being used as a strict benchmark.
privacy: TEST STATE ONLY. Do not publish verbatim text on any public page. Do not attempt to re-identify authors.

post.author: OP
post.text:
Maine faces a projected $1B+ budget gap for 2028–29, and the new governor's budget is due in February.

You're in charge of setting the Maine budget. What would you cut or raise?

I see a lot of talk here attacking and defending fiscal policy. So what would you propose?
Spending cuts? To what program, what amount, and what is the impact?
Tax cuts? Which tax, and what spending would be cut to cover it?
New taxes? Which tax, what rate, how much it raises, and where does the money go?
Fraud/waste? Which program? Link the audit, case, or report.
Let's explore opinions, discuss the impact and the math.

comments.author: R043
comments.text:
First, the projected budget gap is just that. Projected.

Every government budget that I have ever worked on starts out with a projected budget gap.

You begin by working with best guess estimates of revenue and expenses. You start with flat funding from the year before, with increases for known inflation (fuel, labor, insurances, etc.)

And then you examine the actual numbers of incoming revenue, and then compare them to the projected revenue from earlier estimates.

And then you begin the real hard work of where best to cut and increase both spending AND tax revenues.

That’s why the choice for the Commissioner of Administrative and Financial Services is so important. One of the best at the job was a Republican, Sawin Millett.

And probably the governor-elects most important appointee…
